# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Review: Lindqvist et al., *Two Years On* (Varden 24-month follow-up and Halden subset)

This is the most informative document in the series. It does three things the earlier papers could not:

- It adds a 24-month randomised estimate to the evidence.
- It brings in a second, independent hours measure.
- It tests the meetings hypothesis under a registered plan.

It also corrects the two previous papers fairly and specifically.

**On the meta-analysis.** The authors check its supplementary table and find that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That confirms the concern raised about the meta-analysis's duration claim.

**On the re-analysis.** They meet the re-analysis's own recommended standards and still find a gain whose confidence interval excludes zero.

The remaining problems are specific, and two of them affect the headline numbers:

- The log-hours measure may not measure what it is presented as measuring.
- Contamination in the control arm is reported but never connected to the decay estimate.

## Arithmetic check

| Figure | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% (timesheets, 24 m) | ✓ |
| 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% (logs, 24 m) | ✓ |
| 34.9 / 40.3 | −13.4% hours | ✓ |
| 96.8 / 86.6 | +11.8% (Halden continuers) | ✓ |
| 47 + 18 + 35 | 100% | ✓ |
| Cost per contact +9% from +12% staff | consistent if staff are about 75% of cost | plausible |

## 1. What do "system logs" measure?

The log measure is described as "active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases". If that description is accurate, it measures **time spent on cases**, not total working time. It would then exclude:

- meetings
- email
- phone calls
- training
- any offline file work

This matters in two ways.

**It is not a stricter measure of hours.** Treated offices cut about 3.5 hours a week of meetings. Their case time should therefore have fallen by much less than their total time, possibly by close to nothing. Yet the logs show an 11% fall, against 12% on timesheets. Either the measure includes more than case time, or something else is going on. The paper needs to define exactly what the log records and confirm that a pre-period log baseline exists. The 9-month column is blank, but a difference-in-differences estimate needs pre-period data.

**It makes the mediation hard to interpret.** Cutting meetings raises output per *total* hour mechanically, because non-case time is removed from the denominator. It should not raise output per *case* hour, unless fewer meetings also improve focus. If the outcome is output per case hour, a 47% share through meetings implies a focus or fragmentation effect, not simple removal of low-value time. That is a different and more interesting claim, and it should be stated explicitly. If the outcome is output per total hour, the mechanical part of the effect should be separated from any behavioural part.

## 2. Control contamination probably explains part of the decline

The meeting audit in two control offices is presented as a side observation. But it occurred in month 15, inside the period over which decay is measured.

- Two of seven control offices improved output per hour by about 4.1%.
- On its own, that raises the control mean by roughly 1.2 points.
- The like-for-like decline in the treatment effect, from 12.5% to 9.8%, is about 2.7 points.

So something like 40% of the apparent fading may come from control offices improving rather than treated offices declining. The two control offices may also have been prompted by the nine-month report's meetings finding, which makes this classic contamination.

The paper should do two things:

- Report the treated and control trajectories separately, so readers can see which arm moved.
- Re-estimate the 24-month effect excluding the two audited offices, or truncating them at month 15.

The before-and-after gain in those two offices, compared with their own previous six months, also carries the usual risks of seasonality and regression to the mean.

## 3. The Summary compares different measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data". But 12.5% comes from timesheets and 8.5% from logs. The like-for-like comparison on timesheets is 12.5% to 9.8%, which is a decline of about 22%. Mixing the two measures makes the decline look like about 32%.

Section 5's "about a quarter" matches the timesheet comparison. The Summary should match Section 5. Two further points:

- The decline itself is not tested. The two estimates have heavily overlapping confidence intervals. A within-office test of the change between waves would show whether the decline is distinguishable from noise.
- The rebuttal says the result is "not consistent with falling to zero by month ten". That is fair as a response to Varga & Holm, but their extrapolation used Halden's self-reported energy data. Applying it to Varden is a cross-setting comparison, and the paper should say so.

## 4. The mediation is weaker than "confirms"

- **The hypothesis was tested on the data that generated it.** The meetings hypothesis came from month-6 data in these same 14 offices. A test registered at month 11, run on office-months that include months 1–9, is pre-specified but not independent. Restricting the analysis to months 10–24 would give a cleaner confirmatory test.
- **The effective sample is 14 offices, not the office-months.** The treatment varies only at office level. A 95% CI of 28–66% looks narrow for seven treated offices. State whether standard errors were clustered by office and whether a small-cluster method was used, such as wild cluster bootstrap. That was already a concern at nine months.
- **Confounding of the mediators.** Managers who cut meetings readily may also run their offices better in other ways. The Limitations section acknowledges this in general terms, but it bears directly on the 47% figure.
- **The pathways may not be additive.** Fewer meetings may themselves reduce fatigue. Say whether the model is parallel or sequential, and whether the two shares can sum the way Table 2 implies.
- **Where baseline meeting data came from.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month 6. The 7.4 and 7.2 hours now reported as baseline were presumably reconstructed from calendar histories. Say so, and note any gaps.

"Survives a registered test" is accurate. "Confirms" in the Summary is too strong. Something like "a registered test supports the meetings pathway" would be safer.

## 5. Counter arm: the staffing estimate is probably too low

The county estimated that 12% more staff would restore service. That figure is consistent with inverting output per employee, since 1 / 0.886 ≈ 1.13. But as noted at nine months, counter output depends on demand. Much of the 6.7% per-hour gain was higher utilisation, meaning less idle time, not extra capacity.

Waiting times depend on how many staff are present, so restoring the original waits would need roughly the original staffed hours. That implies something closer to 1 / 0.83 ≈ 20% more staff, unless the gain in output per hour is real capacity. Queueing effects are nonlinear, so the true figure could fall anywhere between these two. The 9% cost estimate should be presented as a lower bound.

## 6. Halden subset

- **Non-response.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations contacted responded, so a non-response filter now sits on top of the earlier survivorship.
- **"Upper bound" is too strong.** Without a comparison group, the 11.8% could be biased in either direction by economic conditions or general trends. "Likely optimistic" is accurate. "Upper bound" is not.
- **The marketing agency doesn't fit the framing.** The Summary says all three reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations", but a marketing agency missing client deadlines is not coverage-bound in the meta-analysis's sense. It is deadline-driven, which the meta-analysis coding counts as discretionary. This suggests a third category, such as client-responsiveness, that the binary split misses. The paper should discuss this rather than absorb it into the coverage story.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Sick days.** The −27% figure is still per FTE. If the hours reduction was implemented as fewer working days, part of the fall is mechanical. Report absence per scheduled day. This has been an open question since nine months.
- **Appeal overturn rates** (3.2% v 3.0%) are still levels with no confidence interval and no difference-in-differences estimate.
- **Few-cluster inference** for Table 1 is still not described.
- **Authorship.** Okafor is a Halden author reporting on Halden organisations, which is worth a disclosure line. This is not a criticism of the analysis.

## Suggested revisions

1. Define the log measure precisely. Report its pre-period baseline and state whether it includes non-case time. Reframe the mediation outcome to match.
2. Report treated and control trajectories separately, and re-estimate the 24-month effect excluding or truncating the two audited control offices.
3. Make the Summary's 9-to-24-month comparison like-for-like, and formally test the change between waves.
4. Run the mediation on months 10–24 only, with small-cluster inference, and soften "confirms".
5. Present the counter-arm cost estimate as a lower bound.
6. Reconsider how the marketing agency's reversion is framed.

## State of the evidence after five documents

- **Per-hour gain.** In discretionary public-sector case work, a randomised estimate is about +8.5–10% at 24 months. It has faded somewhat from nine months, though control contamination may account for a good part of that fading. It is clearly not zero.
- **Output per employee.** In discretionary work it is slightly below control, at about −3%. In coverage-bound work it fell enough that the county ended that arm.
- **Mechanism.** Cutting meetings is the best-supported pathway, and fatigue contributes less. Whether reorganisation without an hours cut could capture most of the gain remains the key untested question. A three-arm trial would answer it: hours cut, meeting audit only, and control.
- **Generalisability.** The evidence rests on one public employer and one self-selected private subset. Deadline-driven client work may form a third category alongside discretionary and coverage-bound work.
